title: King Kisra Anushirwan and the Village Damsel

keywords: king kisra anushirwan and the village damsel
full_text:
King Kisra Anushirwan, celebrated across the chronicles of Persia as 'The Just,' was hunting in a remote province of his empire when he became separated from his retinue. Exhausted and parched with thirst, he rode into a modest village orchard where a young maiden was watering pomegranate trees.

The king dismounted and asked for a draught of water. The maiden smiled with graceful courtesy: 'Water is scarce, O traveler, but wait a moment, and I shall fetch you the sweet juice of our orchard.'

She went into the trees, plucked a single large, ruby-red pomegranate, and squeezed it into a clay bowl. To the king's astonishment, the single fruit yielded a full bowl of clear, deliciously sweet juice! Anushirwan drank with immense delight, finding his strength instantly restored.

Looking around the thriving village, a thought of greed entered the monarch’s mind: 'This orchard is extraordinarily fertile; when I return to the capital, I shall double the taxes on this district to enrich my royal treasury.'

He asked the maiden for a second bowl. She went into the orchard, plucked another pomegranate from the same bough, and squeezed it. But this time, she labored for a long time, and the fruit yielded only a few bitter drops of cloudy juice.

The king was amazed and asked: 'Why was the first fruit so abundant and sweet, while this second fruit from the same tree is so dry and bitter?'

The maiden looked at him with wise, untroubled eyes and replied: 'O traveler, know you not the ancient mystery of our land? When the king’s intention is just and benevolent, the heavens shower blessings, and the fruits overflow with sweetness. But when the king’s heart turns toward greed and oppression, the fertility departs from the earth, and the fruits wither in their rinds!'

Anushirwan’s heart was pierced with profound shame. He repented of his greedy intention, praised the maiden’s wisdom, and rewarded the village with tax exemptions, reaffirming his sacred vow that justice alone must be the crown of a king.
moral: The justice of a king sweetens the fruits of the land, while royal greed brings drought and bitterness.
